title: Learned End-to-End Guidance Schedules for Diffusion Models

paper.title: Learned End-to-End Guidance Schedules for Diffusion Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion models are a powerful generative paradigm used across multimedia and scientific applications.
Guided diffusion methods impose requirements on the generation by adding the gradient of a differentiable loss (the guidance function ) as a drift term during inference.
The weight of this drift (the guidance scale ) is critical for the trade-off between data quality and requirement satisfaction. To achieve both of these goals, guided diffusion must resort to small guidance scales and lengthy sampling, incurring high computational costs.
This work proposes learned end-to-end guidance schedules (LEEGS) to achieve these objectives with fewer sampling steps . LEEGS trains a time-dependent schedule by minimizing the guidance function over a small set of examples using stochastic gradient descent. Backpropagating through guided sampling is computationally expensive, so LEEGS uses an approximation of the gradient that cuts training time by a factor of 4.
We evaluate LEEGS on diverse guidance tasks, including (a) image inpainting, (b) noisy image inverse problems, (c) face-ID-guided generation, and (d) forward and inverse PDE problems, outperforming baselines at equal budget (50 or 100 NFEs), or matching constant guidance with only 10% of the steps.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models have been successful in modeling and generating data across many domains, from multimedia tasks [e.g., image synthesis ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ) , image restoration ( Kawar et al., 2022 ; Chung et al., 2023 ) , text-to-image generation ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Nichol et al., 2022 ) ] to scientific and engineering applications [e.g., molecular generation ( Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2022 ) , protein generation ( Watson et al., 2023 ) , solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs) ( Huang et al., 2024a ; Bastek et al., 2025 ) , design optimization ( Maze & Ahmed, 2023 ) ]. Guided diffusion [e.g., ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ; Bansal et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Corso et al., 2023 ) ] allows these models to produce data satisfying ancillary requirements, such as the physical viability of samples for scientific and engineering applications ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Christopher et al., 2024a ) , or solve inverse problems ( Chung et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024a ) . While several training-free approaches induce a requirement in diffusion models, such as particle-based ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Corso et al., 2023 ) or projection-based methods ( Christopher et al., 2024b ; Christopher et al., 2024a ) , if its violation can be expressed as a differentiable loss h ⁡ ( x ) h(x) (the guidance function ), then modifying the diffusion with a drift − ∇ w h -\nabla_{w}h of strength w > 0 w>0 (the guidance scale ) yields a powerful, general approach [see, e.g. ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ; Bansal et al., 2023 ) ]. Yet, guidance exacerbates a well-known limitation of diffusion models: slow inference. All guidance techniques face a trade-off between data quality (staying close to the model’s learned distribution) and requirement satisfaction (minimizing the violation h h ). Small scales ( w ≪ 1 ) (w\ll 1) do not sufficiently reduce the violation h h , yielding samples that violate the requirements; while large scales ( w ≫ 1 ) (w\gg 1) cause substantial changes to the original diffusion trajectory, yielding unrealistic samples. To generate high-quality data satisfying requirements, guided generation algorithms such as ( Chung et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2023 ) resort to small guidance scales and many inference steps, resulting in high computational cost. Our aim is to reduce the number of steps in the sampling process to balance data quality and the satisfaction of requirements. Different approaches have been proposed to tackle this problem. For instance, Yang et al. (2024) rescales the guidance gradient relative to the sampling noise at each step, enabling larger step sizes and thus shorter trajectories, but still requires choosing a guidance scale. Methods that alternate between denoising and guidance optimization [e.g. ( Zampini et al., 2025 ; Jayaram et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024b ) ] control the deviation explicitly via a trust region or a proximal penalty. However, tuning the trust-region radius or penalty weight is as delicate as tuning the guidance scale itself. A different strategy for mitigating this trade-off has been explored in the classifier-free guidance (CFG) setting, where the guidance scale is made time-dependent ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Sadat et al., 2024 ; Malarz et al., 2025 ) following the observation that constant guidance is suboptimal for CFG ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) . Learning a time-dependent scale has likewise been studied for CFG ( Yehezkel et al., 2025 ; Galashov et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) , but not for loss-based guidance, whose main advantage is that it conditions a pretrained model without retraining. We bring learned time-dependent guidance scales ( guidance schedules ) to loss-guided diffusion, achieving better trade-offs between data quality and requirement satisfaction. LEEGS trains a schedule for a given model, task, and sampler by minimizing the value of the guidance function along the diffusion trajectory, averaged over a small set of examples. This requires backpropagating through the sampling trajectory, a naive implementation of which would incur untenable peak memory and per-batch compute. We use gradient checkpointing to bound the memory cost, similarly to when optimizing other diffusion parameters, such as sampling coefficients ( Watson et al., 2022 ) , discretizations ( Tong et al., 2025 ) , and noise ( Tang et al., 2024 ) . We further propose an approximation of the objective’s gradient that reduces per-batch compute. Put together, these improvements allow LEEGS to effectively manage the guidance trade-off in a tractable manner. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first review guided diffusion sampling in Section 2 , then present our problem formulation and method in Section 3 . We introduce our main empirical results in Section 4 , starting with a description of the applications we consider, namely various guided image generation tasks and PDE problems, followed by further experiments and ablation studies. Finally, we conclude in Section 6 . (a) LEEGS training procedure. The forward pass (computing ℒ ⁡ ( W ) \mathcal{L}(W) ) runs the guided diffusion sampling, while the backward pass (updating W W ) backpropagates the objective through the sampling trajectory. (b) LEEGS achieves convincing inpainting results with only 10 inference steps while constant guidance only reconstructs a plausible-looking but incorrect face even at w = 0.15 w=0.15 , which achieves the optimal LPIPS on a held-out set of 100 images. A larger scale ( w = 2.0 w=2.0 ) does not improve consistency with the unmasked regions, but produces unrealistic, saturated artifacts instead. See Section 4.1 for details on the noisy box-inpainting task.

sections.heading: Regularization.
sections.text: Attempting to drive the guidance function h h too low may occasionally push the guided marginals p W ​ ( x s ∣ c ) p_{W}(x_{s}\mid c) too far from the unguided p ⁡ ( x s ) p(x_{s}) , yielding unrealistic samples, which can be seen as a form of reward hacking ( Tang et al., 2024 ; Zhai et al., 2025 ) . This manifests in Figure 2 as an increase in the LPIPS metric after a certain point in the optimization. This phenomenon can be mitigated either by early stopping, when a held-out reward is available to detect the decline in performance, or by penalizing the magnitude of the guidance schedule W W in the training objective as in, e.g. minimizing ℒ ⁡ ( W ) + γ ​ ‖ W ‖ 2 2 \mathcal{L}(W)+\gamma\,\left\|W\right\|_{2}^{2} with γ > 0 \gamma>0 . Appendix C.3 explores which tasks are prone to reward hacking and how the penalty alleviates it. Typically, even on tasks which are prone to reward hacking, it appears only at high S S (e.g., S = 100 S=100 ), not at lower S S (e.g., S = 25 S=25 ).

sections.heading: Parametrization.
sections.text: LEEGS optimizes the schedule freely over W ∈ ℝ + S W\in\mathbb{R}^{S}_{+} . While W W can be constrained to a parametric family, w s = ρ ϕ ​ ( s ) w_{s}=\rho_{\phi}(s) with ϕ \phi small, trading flexibility for fewer parameters and a smoother schedule, this requires the functional form to be fixed in advance. Since LEEGS’s cost is dominated by the guided sampling, we find this trade-off unnecessary in practice.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate LEEGS on guided image generation and PDE problems, comparing it with baseline methods across budgets and analyzing its schedules, sample efficiency, and sensitivity to sampler choice and inference steps.

sections.heading: Image inpainting.
sections.text: Inpainting seeks to recover a complete image from a partial observation. With condition c = ( y , M ) c=(y,M) , where y y is the observed image and M M a binary mask marking the missing pixels, we consider the guidance function h ⁡ ( x , c ) = ‖ M ⊙ x − y ‖ 2 h(x,c)=\left\|M\odot x-y\right\|_{2} , where ⊙ \odot denotes elementwise multiplication. Unlike projection-renoising methods, such as RePaint ( Lugmayr et al., 2022 ) , which inject the observed pixels directly and can leave visible seams at low step counts, guided sampling enforces the observed pixels softly. We generate synthetic inpainting problems on ImageNet and CelebA-HQ using the five mask types from Lugmayr et al. (2022) : wide and narrow (large or thin contiguous regions are not observed), super-resolution 2 × 2\times (one pixel kept per 2 × 2 2\times 2 block), alternating-lines (every other row removed), and half (right half removed). We compare against RePaint at a matched 200-NFE budget and include the original results using 2400 NFEs from Lugmayr et al. (2022) as a reference. We report LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , the perceptual distance to the ground truth image (lower is better).

sections.heading: Noisy inverse problems.
sections.text: We use image restoration to illustrate an inverse problem ( Kawar et al., 2022 ; Chung et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) with a known degradation operator 𝒜 \mathcal{A} . The noisy measurement of the image x GT x_{\text{GT}} under condition c = ( y , 𝒜 ) c=(y,\mathcal{A}) is y = 𝒜 ⁡ ( x GT ) + σ ​ n y=\mathcal{A}(x_{\text{GT}})+\sigma n , with an unknown noise level σ > 0 \sigma>0 and n ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 ) n\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) . We choose the guidance function as h ⁡ ( x , c ) = ‖ 𝒜 ⁡ ( x ) − y ‖ 2 h(x,c)=\left\|\mathcal{A}(x)-y\right\|_{2} . Following Chung et al. (2023) , we synthesize problems from held-out FFHQ and ImageNet images and evaluate five tasks at σ = 0.05 \sigma=0.05 : 4 × 4\times super-resolution, box inpainting (a large centred square removed), random inpainting (each pixel dropped independently with high probability), and Gaussian and motion deblurring (details of the operators are in App. B ). Unlike the noiseless inpainting benchmark above, the observations here are corrupted, handicapping methods that inject observed pixels directly, such as RePaint. We compare against recent methods for inverse problems (CDIM ( Jayaram et al., 2025 ) , DSG ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , and DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) ) at 50 and 100 NFEs, and include the 1000-NFE DPS ( Chung et al., 2023 ) numbers reported in Chung et al. (2023) as a reference. We also compare against constant guidance and heuristic increasing and decreasing linear schedules, each with a single parameter tuned by grid search on a held-out set (App. B ). Alongside LPIPS, we report FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , the distributional distance between generated samples and a reference set (lower is better).

sections.heading: Face-ID guidance.
sections.text: Following Yu et al. (2023) ; Yang et al. (2024) , we generate images of a target identity given a single reference photo x ref x_{\text{ref}} (the condition c c ), using the guidance function h ⁡ ( x , x ref ) = ‖ F ⁡ ( x ) − F ⁡ ( x ref ) ‖ 2 h(x,x_{\text{ref}})=\left\|F(x)-F(x_{\text{ref}})\right\|_{2} , where F F is the feature embedding of a pretrained face-recognition network [we use the ArcFace model ( Deng et al., 2019 ) ]. Such a network embeds faces so that images of the same person lie close together, so minimizing h h steers the generated image toward the reference identity. We compare against constant guidance and DSG ( Yang et al., 2024 ) on CelebA-HQ at 50 and 100 NFEs. We report FID and the guidance value itself, the FaceID score (identity distance to the reference, lower is better).

sections.heading: PDE problems.
sections.text: Diffusion models can solve partial differential equations (PDEs) from sparse observations, complementing classical ( Trefethen, 1996 ; Langtangen & Mardal, 2019 ) and learned ( Raissi et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2020 ) solvers. Following DiffusionPDE ( Huang et al., 2024a ) , we consider boundary-value problems specified by a coefficient field a a and its solution field u u . The diffusion model is pretrained on a dataset of solved instances and represents the joint distribution over coefficient–solution pairs ( a , u ) (a,u) rendered as images. Given observations { a obs , i } i = 1 N obs \{a_{\text{obs},i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\text{obs}}} of the coefficient at locations { z obs , i } i = 1 N obs \{z_{\text{obs},i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\text{obs}}} , the inverse-problem guidance function is h inv ​ ( x , c ) = 1 N obs ​ ∑ i = 1 N obs ( a ⁡ ( z obs , i ) − a obs , i ) 2 h_{\text{inv}}(x,c)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N_{\text{obs}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{obs}}}\left(a(z_{\text{obs},i})-a_{\text{obs},i}\right)^{2}} with condition c = ( a obs , z obs ) c=(a_{\text{obs}},z_{\text{obs}}) ; the forward guidance function is defined analogously on the solution field, h fwd ​ ( x , c ) = 1 N obs ​ ∑ i = 1 N obs ( u ⁡ ( z obs , i ) − u obs , i ) 2 h_{\text{fwd}}(x,c)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N_{\text{obs}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{obs}}}\left(u(z_{\text{obs},i})-u_{\text{obs},i}\right)^{2}} with condition c = ( u obs , z obs ) c=(u_{\text{obs}},z_{\text{obs}}) . We evaluate forward (recover u u from a a ) and inverse (recover a a from u u ) problems for the Helmholtz, Poisson, and Darcy equations, with ≈ 3 % \approx 3\% of pixels observed. We compare against constant guidance and heuristic increasing and decreasing linear schedules at 50 and 100 steps, and include the DiffusionPDE ( Huang et al., 2024a ) results at 2000 steps as a reference. While DiffusionPDE additionally applies a PDE-residual guidance term over a small part of the trajectory, we found little benefit from it and omit it for both constant guidance and LEEGS. sections.heading: 4.2 Main results
sections.text: For each task and step budget, LEEGS trains a guidance schedule on 30 examples drawn from a training pool disjoint from the corresponding test set, using Adam with batch size 1 and training separately for every subtask and NFE budget. This pool has 90 images for every task except FFHQ, where we instead use a cross-validation-style split. All evaluations (except reference rows taken from original works) used test sets of size: 950 for FFHQ (Table 1 ); 1000 for ImageNet noisy inverse problems (Table 2 ); 100 for the inpainting and Face-ID tasks (Tables 3 and 4 ); and 1000 for Helmholtz and Darcy, 924 for Poisson, for the PDE problems (Table 5 ). Exact training and dataset details (e.g., learning rates, epochs, pretrained models) are given in App. B . All results for LEEGS are the mean of three independent runs (with randomly drawn training sets).

sections.heading: Noisy inverse problems.
sections.text: Tables 1 and 2 report LPIPS and FID on FFHQ and ImageNet. On FFHQ, LEEGS is the best or second-best method in nearly every column at both 50 and 100 NFE, with the best LPIPS on four of the five subtasks. On ImageNet, LEEGS is best or second-best in every column at both 50 and 100 NFE, and the best in 4 out of 5 subtasks for ImageNet at 100 NFE with respect to both metrics. The tuned linear- increasing schedule is itself a strong heuristic here, while linear- decreasing is consistently poor, illustrating that effective schedule shapes are task-dependent (Fig. 3 ) and LEEGS recovers a good one without that prior. LEEGS at 100 NFE also beats the 1000-NFE DPS reference on both LPIPS and FID for most subtasks, a 10 × 10\times reduction in steps.

sections.heading: Image inpainting.
sections.text: At a matched 200-NFE budget, LEEGS improves over RePaint on every mask type and both datasets (Table 3 ); RePaint with 12 × 12\times the budget stays ahead on most masks.

sections.heading: Face-ID guidance.
sections.text: Table 4 reports FaceID similarity and FID for guided face generation. At 50 NFE, all three rows are similar, except DSG’s FID which is significantly worse. However, at 100 NFE, LEEGS performs best on both metrics, improving over DSG and constant guidance.

sections.heading: PDE problems.
sections.text: LEEGS attains the lowest relative error on 4 of the 6 forward/inverse problems at 50 sampling steps, and on 5 of 6 at 100 steps (Table 5 ), in both cases at half the NFE of the constant-guidance baseline (which runs a second-order sampler). However, DiffusionPDE’s results, which use 20 × 20\times more steps, retain an advantage. The linear- decreasing schedule remains a strong fixed baseline here: it is in fact the best method for the inverse Darcy problem at both step budgets, and for the Darcy forward problem at 50 steps, though the same heuristic is among the worst on the noisy-inverse tasks, where linear- increasing dominates instead. Which fixed shape works is task- and problem-specific and not knowable in advance; LEEGS matches or outperforms both heuristics on most problems.

sections.heading: Learned schedules.
sections.text: Figure 3 shows example schedules learned by LEEGS. For a given problem they have a similar shape across step budgets, but they differ substantially between problems: increasing schedules help the noisy inverse problems, whereas decreasing schedules help the PDE tasks, mirroring the performance of the linear-schedule baselines in Tables 1 , 2 , and 5 . Schedules differ even between closely related tasks: among the five FFHQ inverse problems, App. C.4 shows that the schedule learned for a task is best on that task in nearly every case, motivating the need for a learned, task-specific schedule.

sections.heading: Beyond DPS-style sampling.
sections.text: LEEGS requires only a differentiable sampling trajectory and makes no assumption on the form of the sampler. Beyond stochastic (DDPM; Tables 1 , 2 , 3 ) and deterministic (Euler; Table 5 ) samplers, we apply it without modification to a sampler that alternates guided reverse diffusion with renoising , a common ingredient of inverse-problem solvers such as RePaint ( Lugmayr et al., 2022 ) , DDNM ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , and DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . App. D shows that this sampling scheme when combined with LEEGS can perform competitively with the vanilla version of LEEGS on the FFHQ inverse problems (with better results for box and random inpainting), highlighting the flexibility of LEEGS. Moreover, the learned schedules for this scheme consist of a sequence of hill-shaped segments (Fig. 17 ). Such a schedule would be hard to recover even with a priori knowledge, while the cost of learning them with LEEGS is unchanged.

sections.heading: Effect of inference steps.
sections.text: LEEGS generally improves with more inference steps, with diminishing returns (Tables 1 – 5 ; App. C.5 ). As the budget grows, the mean guidance weight decreases monotonically (Fig. 3 ): more steps need less aggressive per-step guidance. Since the schedule’s shape is largely shared across budgets and its magnitude follows a predictable trend, a schedule trained at small S S can be interpolated and rescaled to larger S S at inference time, offering a way to reduce the training cost at large S S (App. C.5 ).

sections.heading: Sample efficiency.
sections.text: LEEGS is trained on only 30 30 examples per subtask. Both the learned schedule and the resulting test performance are largely insensitive to the size of the training set, changing little beyond 30 30 samples (App. C.1 ).

sections.heading: Guidance scheduling (for CFG).
sections.text: CFG ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) steers a conditional diffusion model toward a condition y y (e.g., a class label or text embedding) by combining the conditional and unconditional noise predictions ϵ θ ​ ( x s , y ) \epsilon_{\theta}(x_{s},y) and ϵ θ ​ ( x s , ∅ ) \epsilon_{\theta}(x_{s},\emptyset) ( ∅ \emptyset the null condition) with a guidance scale w w . As in our setting, w w must be chosen, and can be varied over the course of generation. Several works vary the CFG scale over the trajectory. It was shown by Kynkäänniemi et al. (2024) that a nontrivial scale ( w ≠ 1 w\neq 1 ) is only needed within a limited interval, with the conditional noise prediction ϵ θ ​ ( x s , y ) \epsilon_{\theta}(x_{s},y) used alone elsewhere. Fixed schedules were compared and proposed by Wang et al. (2024) ; Sadat et al. (2024) ; Malarz et al. (2025) , and adaptive per-step scales have been derived from the two noise predictions ( Zhu et al., 2026 ; Pavasovic et al., 2025 ) , from estimated log-likelihoods ( Koulischer et al., 2025 ) , or by a stepwise greedy search ( Papalampidi et al., 2025 ) . Methods that learn the guidance scale [e.g., ( Yehezkel et al., 2025 ; Galashov et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Azangulov et al., 2026 ) ] are closest to our work. Azangulov et al. (2026) is a primarily theoretical work in which the guidance scale is learned as a function of the sample x s x_{s} by optimizing an optimal-control objective. Yehezkel et al. (2025) ; Galashov et al. (2025) learn guidance networks that predict the CFG guidance scale as a function of the intermediate sample x s x_{s} and time t s t_{s} . The training objectives of these methods do not use rewards and instead rely on labeled data. Sun et al. (2025) uses an evolutionary search to learn a sparse guidance schedule supervised by a constant-guidance reference process; this is expensive, requiring many 1000-step reference rollouts. To our knowledge, LEEGS is the first to learn guidance schedules for loss-guided diffusion.

sections.heading: Constrained diffusion.
sections.text: Constrained diffusion methods interpret the guidance function h h as a constraint function and seek to minimize it, as in our setting. These include projection ( Christopher et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Christopher et al., 2024a ) , trust-sampling ( Huang et al., 2024b ) , proximal ( Zampini et al., 2025 ; Jayaram et al., 2025 ) , and consensus ( Christopher et al., 2026 ; Blanke et al., 2026 ) methods. Projection-based methods ensure constraint satisfaction, but closed-form projections are typically only available for convex constraints, so several methods approximate them with an inner optimization loop ( Christopher et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, projections take arbitrarily large guidance steps, which can deviate substantially from the distribution induced by the diffusion model; this is typically mitigated by renoising the projected sample, which lengthens the sampling process. Proximal and trust-region sampling methods explicitly address the guidance trade-off by optimizing the constraint only up to a threshold, or within a fixed distance of the denoised iterate. However, the threshold or radius is itself a hyperparameter as delicate to set as the guidance scale. Consensus-based methods take another approach, splitting inference into two trajectories (one applying projections, one following the unguided reverse process) and annealing them to coincide by the end of sampling. A guidance term implicitly pulls the trajectories together, and Blanke et al. (2026) sets its scale by dual ascent. Consensus methods are closely related to guidance and could be combined with LEEGS. Unlike the projection- and threshold-based methods above, though, LEEGS neither projects nor renoises: it learns a single schedule offline and applies it during ordinary guided sampling at no extra cost.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: LEEGS is a simple, general method for learning time-dependent guidance schedules for loss-guided diffusion. It trains a schedule on as few as 30 examples by backpropagating the guidance loss through the sampler. Across image inpainting, noisy inverse problems, face-ID guidance, and PDE problems (Section 4 ), it is competitive with strong task-specific baselines and matches the 1000-NFE DPS reference using only 100 steps. Two findings stand out: a learned schedule beats constant guidance at a matched budget, and the useful schedule shape is task-dependent, so it should be learned, not fixed by heuristic. LEEGS is also robust to sampler choice, working with stochastic (DDPM) and deterministic (Euler) samplers alike.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Training cost for LEEGS grows with the number of steps S S (the objective spans the full trajectory), making very large S S costly. While our gradient approximation (Section 3 ) is efficient, it may be less effective when the guidance field is highly sensitive to x s x_{s} . Finally, while we learn a task-specific schedule; adapting it to the condition or initial noise remains open.

sections.text: Unless noted otherwise, LEEGS is trained with Adam and batch size 1, separately for each subtask and NFE budget, on 30 examples randomly drawn from a training pool that is disjoint from the test set. sections.heading: Dataset generation.
sections.text: We follow the implementation and settings of Chung et al. (2023) for both FFHQ and ImageNet, which we recap for completeness; Figure 4 illustrates the five measurement operators. For superresolution, the low-resolution images are generated by bicubic downsampling at 4 × 4\times scale. For Gaussian deblurring, the images are convolved with a 61 × 61 61\times 61 Gaussian kernel with standard deviation 3.0 3.0 . For motion deblurring, the images are convolved with a 61 × 61 61\times 61 motion-blur kernel of intensity 0.5 0.5 , generated with the implementation from https://github.com/LeviBorodenko/motionblur . For box and random inpainting, the masks are sampled randomly for each image, where for box inpainting the mask is an approximately centered 128 × 128 128\times 128 square, and for random inpainting the mask is a random binary mask with each pixel masked with a probability of 0.92 0.92 . For FFHQ, we use the test set of 1000 1000 images of Chung et al. (2023) for training and validation. For the other datasets, we set aside a disjoint pool of 100 100 images ( 90 90 for training and 10 10 for validation metrics during training), but for FFHQ we use a cross-validation-style split of the 1000 1000 images instead, to maintain a reasonable test set size : the first 50 50 images are set aside, of which the first 30 30 are used to train LEEGS and the remaining 20 20 for validation, and the other 950 950 images form the test set of Table 1 . For ImageNet, we build our own training and test sets. The test set of Table 2 consists of 1000 1000 images sampled from the ILSVRC 2012 validation set, one per class, and a disjoint pool of 100 100 images is split into 90 90 images for training, from which each LEEGS run draws 30 30 , and 10 10 for validation.

sections.text: This section analyzes the variance in the learned guidance schedule due to the choice of training set. We consider two tasks : the noisy motion deblur on FFHQ, and the Helmholtz forward PDE problem, both at S = 10 S=10 . We train the guidance schedule on datasets of varying size n n , where each dataset is drawn randomly from a larger pool of 500 500 samples. For each n n we draw 10 10 datasets and train a separate guidance schedule on each, holding the total number of training iterations fixed as n n varies. For both tasks, we sweep n ∈ { 1 , 5 , 30 , 50 , 100 } n\in\{1,5,30,50,100\} . We evaluate each learned schedule on a held-out test set of 300 300 samples, reporting the reconstruction quality [LPIPS for FFHQ, relative L 2 L_{2} error with respect to u u (the solution) for Helmholtz forward; see Figure 6 ] and the per-draw distance of the learned schedule from the draw-averaged schedule (see Figure 7 ). The latter metric directly measures the variability of the schedule, while the former measures its effect on overall performance. We also plot the mean of the learned schedules across the 10 10 draws for different n n in Figure 8 . We see that the variance with respect to both metrics decreases with increasing n n . While the evaluation metrics plateau at larger n n for both tasks, the variability of the learned schedules continues to decrease for the Helmholtz forward problem. This could be due to the use of a deterministic sampler for the PDE problem, which reduces the variance of the learned schedule. In contrast, the FFHQ motion deblur task uses a stochastic sampler, which introduces additional variability in the learned schedule. Figure 8 shows that the mean schedule is relatively stable across n n , especially for the FFHQ motion deblur task. Note that this is not a measure of variance, but the trend in the average schedule learned across the 10 10 draws for each n n . This observation seems to imply that training with fewer samples has more variance and less bias, with respect to the mean schedule learned with larger datasets. sections.heading: C.3 Effect of regularization
sections.text: This section studies the effect of weight decay on the end-to-end LEEGS guidance schedule, and its interaction with the number of diffusion steps S S . We consider two FFHQ inverse tasks that behave differently under prolonged training: superresolution , where we observe an overfitting elbow in which the terminal constraint keeps improving while held-out reconstruction quality worsens, and box inpainting , where no such elbow appears. For each task we train the guidance schedule with the Adam optimizer’s weight decay ( wdecay ) applied to the guidance-schedule parameters, sweeping wdecay ∈ { 0 , 10 − 5 , 10 − 4 , 5 × 10 − 4 ​ 10 − 3 } \text{wdecay}\in\{0,10^{-5},10^{-4},5\times 10^{-4}\,10^{-3}\} across S ∈ { 10 , 25 , 50 , 100 } S\in\{10,25,50,100\} diffusion steps, for a total of 20 20 configurations per task. We train using a fixed set of 30 30 samples for all runs. The learning rate and number of training epochs are fixed per task and S S . For superresolution, we use a learning rate of 0.3 0.3 and train for 30 30 epochs at S ∈ { 10 , 25 } S\in\{10,25\} , 25 25 epochs at S = 50 S=50 , and 15 15 epochs at S = 100 S=100 . For the box inpainting task we train for 20 epochs with a learning rate of 0.3 0.3 for S = 10 S=10 , 25 25 epochs with a learning rate of 0.3 0.3 for S = 25 S=25 , and 25 25 epochs with a learning rate of 0.2 0.2 for S ∈ { 50,100 } S\in\{50,100\} . Figure 11: Held-out LPIPS as a function of weight decay γ \gamma , one curve per S S (discrete colorbar). Left: superresolution. Right: box inpainting. We evaluate each learned schedule on the held-out test set of 300 300 samples, reporting LPIPS between the reconstruction and the ground-truth image. Figure 2 in the main text shows the corresponding training LPIPS at S = 100 S=100 : without weight decay, training exhibits a sharp reward-hacking elbow, past which the terminal constraint keeps improving while the reconstruction degrades. Increasing weight decay progressively flattens this elbow, and at γ = 5 × 10 − 4 \gamma=5\times 10^{-4} it disappears entirely. The resulting training LPIPS, however, never reaches the value attained just before the unregularized elbow, so early stopping at that point is another fix for this failure mode. Figure 11 (left) shows the analogous picture for superresolution with respect to the LPIPS on the held-out 300 sample test set. At S = 100 S=100 , held-out LPIPS improves with weight decay up to γ = 5 × 10 − 4 \gamma=5\times 10^{-4} , then turns back up at γ = 10 − 3 \gamma=10^{-3} , placing the optimum at 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} rather than at the largest weight decay tried. The same effect appears at S = 50 S=50 , but weaker, with the optimum instead at γ = 10 − 4 \gamma=10^{-4} . At S = 10 , 25 S=10,25 , held-out LPIPS increases monotonically with weight decay: with fewer diffusion steps, the schedule cannot overoptimize the constraint function to begin with, so regularization only costs reconstruction quality. Box inpainting (Figure 11 , right) is comparatively flat: held-out LPIPS is largely insensitive to weight decay across all S S , except at γ = 10 − 3 \gamma=10^{-3} , where it clearly hurts, except at S = 10 S=10 where it remains flat.

sections.heading: C.4 Generalization across tasks
sections.text: This section asks whether a guidance schedule learned for one task generalizes to other tasks, or equivalently, whether task-specific training is beneficial. We study this on the five FFHQ noisy inverse tasks in three parts: we compare the learned schedules, evaluate each schedule on every other task, and repeat this evaluation after matching the schedule magnitudes to isolate the effect of shape. All schedules are the LEEGS runs (first draw) used for Table 1 at S ∈ { 50,100 } S\in\{50,100\} ; training details are given in Appendix B (Table 7 ). Learned schedules for ImageNet and the PDE tasks are given in Appendix G . sections.heading: Learned schedules.
sections.text: Figure 12 (left) shows that the learned schedules differ in magnitude: box inpainting and the two deblur tasks cluster together, superresolution is larger, and random inpainting has by far the largest guidance. To compare shapes independently of magnitude, Figure 12 (right) divides each schedule by its mean. The shapes also differ, consistently across both S S : gaussian deblur rises roughly linearly over the second half of the trajectory, while superresolution and random inpainting rise earliest and level off or drop towards the end, with a sharp drop in the final steps for random inpainting. Superresolution appears to differ the most with respect to shape from the other tasks, with a much more gradual slope as well as a hill shape. sections.heading: Cross-task transfer.
sections.text: To test how much these differences matter in practice, we sample with the schedule learned for each task (row) under the measurement operator of every task (column), giving a 5 × 5 5\times 5 matrix for each S S . Each cell is evaluated on the same fixed subset of 300 300 images of the test set of Table 1 ; the diagonal is re-evaluated on this subset and therefore differs slightly from the Table 1 . Figure 13 (left) shows that the matched schedule is best in 4 4 of the 5 5 columns at both S S . The exception is motion deblur, where the gaussian deblur schedule wins, but the two are nearly identical ( 0.209 0.209 vs. 0.212 0.212 at S = 50 S=50 , 0.177 0.177 vs. 0.179 0.179 at S = 100 S=100 ). This is expected, since both tasks blur the image with a convolution kernel under the same noise model, and their learned schedules are close in magnitude.

sections.heading: Magnitude-matched transfer.
sections.text: Part of the transfer gap is a magnitude mismatch, most visibly for the random inpainting schedule applied to the deblur tasks. To isolate the effect of shape, we multiply each off-diagonal schedule by a scalar such that its mean guidance over the trajectory equals that of the target task’s learned schedule, which leaves the shape unchanged. The diagonal has a factor of 1 1 and is reused. Figure 13 (right) shows a mixed result, and the matched schedule no longer has a clear advantage. For most target tasks the columns flatten out (e.g. 0.242 0.242 – 0.247 0.247 for gaussian deblur at S = 50 S=50 ). Random inpainting is the exception: the random inpainting and superresolution schedules perform best ( 0.196 0.196 , 0.217 0.217 at S = 50 S=50 ; 0.173 0.173 , 0.171 0.171 at S = 100 S=100 ), while the other three remain substantially worse ( ≥ 0.242 \geq 0.242 ). These are the two schedules that rise earliest and turn down towards the end (Figure 12 , right). Box inpainting is also selective: its own schedule remains best on its task at both S S after rescaling. In summary, task-specific training pays off: the learned schedule is best on its own task in nearly every case, and both of its components (magnitude and shape) matter. The magnitude, which differs by up to a factor of four across tasks, is learned jointly with the shape, and for some tasks (here, random and box inpainting) the task-specific shape gives a further advantage that remains even after matching magnitudes.

sections.heading: C.5 Generalization across number of steps
sections.text: In this section we investigate how similar the guidance schedules learned at different numbers of steps S S are, and whether a schedule learned at one S S generalizes to a larger S S without retraining. The latter goal may especially be helpful in practical applications where training is especially expensive, e.g. due to a large diffusion backbone. We consider two tasks: FFHQ box inpainting and the Helmholtz forward PDE problem.

sections.text: For each task we train a separate schedule at every S ∈ { 10 , 20 , 30 , 50 , 100 } S\in\{10,20,30,50,100\} , with all other hyperparameters fixed to the task’s main-results configuration (Appendix B ). sections.heading: Interpolation and rescaling.
sections.text: Tables 13 and 14 show that plain interpolation performs well for small gaps between S src S_{\text{src}} and S tgt S_{\text{tgt}} , often matching or even beating the trained schedule (the latter could indicate that the guidance magnitude for the target had not yet converged to the optimal value), but degrades as the gap grows. sections.text: This section studies the effect of dropping the non-terminal (trajectory-level) constraint term from the training objective, keeping only the terminal constraint h ⁡ ( x 0 , c ) h(x_{0},c) , where x 0 x_{0} is the final denoised sample. In Section 3 we motivated the trajectory objective by noting that the terminal constraint’s gradient with respect to the guidance scale w s w_{s} decays for steps s s far from the end of the trajectory, so a terminal-only objective gives it progressively less usable training signal as the trajectory gets longer. We now verify this intuition empirically for the box inpainting task on FFHQ, using the same training setup as in the cross-step-budget experiment of Appendix C.5 . We reuse the trained schedules from the cross-step-budget experiment of Appendix C.5 ( S ∈ { 10 , 20 , 30 , 50 , 100 } S\in\{10,20,30,50,100\} for box inpainting, which wer trained for 30 30 epochs each with the full LEEGS objective ℒ ⁡ ( W ) \mathcal{L}(W) (which we call "Trajectory"). sections.heading: Appendix D Extension to sampling with renoising
sections.text: This section applies LEEGS to a sampler that alternates guided reverse diffusion with renoising, i.e. forward diffusion back to a noisier state. Renoising is used by, e.g., RePaint ( Lugmayr et al., 2022 ) , DDNM ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , which calls it time travel, and DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . We denote this variant LEEGS-renoise, and the standard DPS-style sampling used in the rest of the paper simply LEEGS. Using normalized diffusion time τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \uptau\in[0,1] ( 0 0 : noisiest, 1 1 : clean), the sampler splits the S S guided steps into K K outer steps of S / K S/K inner steps each. Outer step j = 0 , … , K − 1 j=0,\ldots,K-1 starts at τ = j / K \uptau=j/K and reverse-diffuses with guidance to the clean end τ = 1 \uptau=1 over S / K S/K uniformly spaced steps. The resulting sample is then renoised in without guidance, to the start τ = ( j + 1 ) / K \uptau=(j+1)/K of the next outer step, using the forward process. The sampler therefore moves back and forth between the clean and noisy ends, with progressively later starting points after each outer step. Thus, each outer step also covers a shorter interval with finer steps than the previous one. The final sample is the output of the last outer step. The learned schedule has one weight per guided step, i.e. S S weights in total, and the NFE budget is the same as for LEEGS with S S steps, since renoising requires no network evaluation. For example, in Figure 17 (box inpainting), the five outer steps start at τ = 0 , 0.2 , 0.4 , 0.6 , 0.8 \uptau=0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8 , and each has its own 10 10 weights. sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: This experiment shows that the main idea of this paper (learning time dependent guidance scales to minimize guidance functions by backpropagating through the sampling trajectory) is applicable to diverse scenarios beyond DPS-style sampling. Moreover, while DPS-style sampling may admit competitive simple schedules, such as the increasing linear schedule in Table 1 , it is much harder to tune or approximate a schedule by hand for a sampler with renoising, whose schedule is a sequence of per-outer-step segments. For LEEGS, the cost is the same in both cases, since it depends only on the number of NFEs in the sampling trajectory.

O. Chamon Affiliation: École polytechnique, Institut Polytechnique de Paris Abstract Diffusion models are a powerful generative paradigm used across multimedia and scientific applications. Guided diffusion methods impose requirements on the generation by adding the gradient of a differentiable loss (the guidance function ) as a drift term during inference. The weight of this drift (the guidance scale ) is critical for the trade-off between data quality and requirement satisfaction. To achieve both of these goals, guided diffusion must resort to small guidance scales and lengthy sampling, incurring high computational costs. This work proposes learned end-to-end guidance schedules (LEEGS) to achieve these objectives with fewer sampling steps . LEEGS trains a time-dependent schedule by minimizing the guidance function over a small set of examples using stochastic gradient descent. Backpropagating through guided sampling is computationally expensive, so LEEGS uses an approximation of the gradient that cuts training time by a factor of 4. We evaluate LEEGS on diverse guidance tasks, including (a) image inpainting, (b) noisy image inverse problems, (c) face-ID-guided generation, and (d) forward and inverse PDE problems, outperforming baselines at equal budget (50 or 100 NFEs), or matching constant guidance with only 10% of the steps. 1 Introduction Diffusion models have been successful in modeling and generating data across many domains, from multimedia tasks [e.g., image synthesis ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ) , image restoration ( Kawar et al., 2022 ; Chung et al., 2023 ) , text-to-image generation ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Nichol et al., 2022 ) ] to scientific and engineering applications [e.g., molecular generation ( Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2022 ) , protein generation ( Watson et al., 2023 ) , solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs) ( Huang et al., 2024a ; Bastek et al., 2025 ) , design optimization ( Maze & Ahmed, 2023 ) ]. Guided diffusion [e.g., ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ; Bansal et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Corso et al., 2023 ) ] allows these models to produce data satisfying ancillary requirements, such as the physical viability of samples for scientific and engineering applications ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Christopher et al., 2024a ) , or solve inverse problems ( Chung et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024a ) . While several training-free approaches induce a requirement in diffusion models, such as particle-based ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Corso et al., 2023 ) or projection-based methods ( Christopher et al., 2024b ; Christopher et al., 2024a ) , if its violation can be expressed as a differentiable loss h ⁡ ( x ) h(x) (the guidance function ), then modifying the diffusion with a drift − ∇ w h -
abla_{w}h of strength w > 0 w>0 (the guidance scale ) yields a powerful, general approach [see, e.g. ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ; Bansal et al., 2023 ) ]. Yet, guidance exacerbates a well-known limitation of diffusion models: slow inference. All guidance techniques face a trade-off between data quality (staying close to the model’s learned distribution) and requirement satisfaction (minimizing the violation h h ). Small scales ( w ≪ 1 ) (w\ll 1) do not sufficiently reduce the violation h h , yielding samples that violate the requirements; while large scales ( w ≫ 1 ) (w\gg 1) cause substantial changes to the original diffusion trajectory, yielding unrealistic samples. To generate high-quality data satisfying requirements, guided generation algorithms such as ( Chung et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2023 ) resort to small guidance scales and many inference steps, resulting in high computational cost. Our aim is to reduce the number of steps in the sampling process to balance data quality and the satisfaction of requirements. Different approaches have been proposed to tackle this problem. For instance, Yang et al. (2024) rescales the guidance gradient relative to the sampling noise at each step, enabling larger step sizes and thus shorter trajectories, but still requires choosing a guidance scale. Methods that alternate between denoising and guidance optimization [e.g. ( Zampini et al., 2025 ; Jayaram et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024b ) ] control the deviation explicitly via a trust region or a proximal penalty. However, tuning the trust-region radius or penalty weight is as delicate as tuning the guidance scale itself. A different strategy for mitigating this trade-off has been explored in the classifier-free guidance (CFG) setting, where the guidance scale is made time-dependent ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Sadat et al., 2024 ; Malarz et al., 2025 ) following the observation that constant guidance is suboptimal for CFG ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) . Learning a time-dependent scale has likewise been studied for CFG ( Yehezkel et al., 2025 ; Galashov et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) , but not for loss-based guidance, whose main advantage is that it conditions a pretrained model without retraining. We bring learned time-dependent guidance scales ( guidance schedules ) to loss-guided diffusion, achieving better trade-offs between data quality and requirement satisfaction. LEEGS trains a schedule for a given model, task, and sampler by minimizing the value of the guidance function along the diffusion trajectory, averaged over a small set of examples. This requires backpropagating through the sampling trajectory, a naive implementation of which would incur untenable peak memory and per-batch compute. We use gradient checkpointing to bound the memory cost, similarly to when optimizing other diffusion parameters, such as sampling coefficients ( Watson et al., 2022 ) , discretizations ( Tong et al., 2025 ) , and noise ( Tang et al., 2024 ) . We further propose an approximation of the objective’s gradient that reduces per-batch compute. Put together, these improvements allow LEEGS to effectively manage the guidance trade-off in a tractable manner. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first review guided diffusion sampling in Section 2 , then present our problem formulation and method in Section 3 . We introduce our main empirical results in Section 4 , starting with a description of the applications we consider, namely various guided image generation tasks and PDE problems, followed by further experiments and ablation studies. Finally, we conclude in Section 6 . (a) LEEGS training procedure. The forward pass (computing ℒ ⁡ ( W ) \mathcal{L}(W) ) runs the guided diffusion sampling, while the backward pass (updating W W ) backpropagates the objective through the sampling trajectory. (b) LEEGS achieves convincing inpainting results with only 10 inference steps while constant guidance only reconstructs a plausible-looking but incorrect face even at w = 0.15 w=0.15 , which achieves the optimal LPIPS on a held-out set of 100 images. To our knowledge, LEEGS is the first to learn guidance schedules for loss-guided diffusion. Constrained diffusion. Constrained diffusion methods interpret the guidance function h h as a constraint function and seek to minimize it, as in our setting. These include projection ( Christopher et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Christopher et al., 2024a ) , trust-sampling ( Huang et al., 2024b ) , proximal ( Zampini et al., 2025 ; Jayaram et al., 2025 ) , and consensus ( Christopher et al., 2026 ; Blanke et al., 2026 ) methods. Projection-based methods ensure constraint satisfaction, but closed-form projections are typically only available for convex constraints, so several methods approximate them with an inner optimization loop ( Christopher et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, projections take arbitrarily large guidance steps, which can deviate substantially from the distribution induced by the diffusion model; this is typically mitigated by renoising the projected sample, which lengthens the sampling process. Proximal and trust-region sampling methods explicitly address the guidance trade-off by optimizing the constraint only up to a threshold, or within a fixed distance of the denoised iterate. However, the threshold or radius is itself a hyperparameter as delicate to set as the guidance scale. Consensus-based methods take another approach, splitting inference into two trajectories (one applying projections, one following the unguided reverse process) and annealing them to coincide by the end of sampling. A guidance term implicitly pulls the trajectories together, and Blanke et al. (2026) sets its scale by dual ascent. Consensus methods are closely related to guidance and could be combined with LEEGS. Unlike the projection- and threshold-based methods above, though, LEEGS neither projects nor renoises: it learns a single schedule offline and applies it during ordinary guided sampling at no extra cost. 6 Conclusion LEEGS is a simple, general method for learning time-dependent guidance schedules for loss-guided diffusion.
